title: The van 't Hoff Equation
lead: An equilibrium constant changes with temperature, and the reaction enthalpy decides which way. Writing the standard Gibbs energy as enthalpy minus temperature times entropy turns ln K into a function of 1/T that can be read off a plot.
notes: The book prints no credits for this page; its two van 't Hoff plots (Figure 26.7.1) are Wikipedia's, used with permission.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here; the one exercise is new and AI-written, with an AI solution checked by computation.

exercises.source_id: we can translate a $K$ value at one temperature into another
exercises.prompt: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), $K = 5.8 \times 10^{5}$ at 298.15 K and $\Delta_rH^\circ = -91.8$ kJ/mol, twice the enthalpy of formation of NH3. Taking $\Delta_rH^\circ$ as constant, estimate $K$ at 400 K.

answer.hint: Use the integrated form with $T_1 = 298.15$ K and $T_2 = 400$ K.
answer.solution:
$\ln \dfrac{K(T_2)}{K(T_1)} = \dfrac{-\Delta H^o}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_2} - \dfrac{1}{T_1}\right) = \dfrac{91\,800\ \text{J/mol}}{8.314\ \text{J/(K mol)}}\left(\dfrac{1}{400\ \text{K}} - \dfrac{1}{298.15\ \text{K}}\right) = -9.43$.

So $K(400\ \text{K}) = (5.8 \times 10^{5})\,e^{-9.43} = 47$. The reaction is exothermic, so heating it lowers $K$ by a factor of about 12 000.
